provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of jss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall previous grammar concepts.
The students should be able to answer comprehension questions.
Introduction:
Last term we studied many grammar rules and comprehension skills. Today we will revise these important topics to strengthen our foundation.
Content:
We will start with comprehension passages about everyday Nigerian life like buying goods at the market. Then we will review grammar points like tenses, parts of speech, and sentence construction. For vocabulary, we will practice words used in different contexts like 'chap' for food and 'dash' for giving something extra.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to read a short passage about a Nigerian market scene and answer questions together.
Evaluation questions:
What are the three main parts of speech?
How do you identify the main idea in a comprehension passage?
Give an example of a formal word and its informal equivalent.
Summary:
Today's revision helps us remember what we learned last term and prepares us for new topics this term.

topics.title: Comprehension: the price of honesty
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to read and comprehend a passage.
The students should be able to summarize paragraphs accurately.
Introduction:
We have practiced reading comprehension before. Today we will read a story about honesty and learn how to find the main points in each paragraph.
Content:
The story 'The price of honesty' tells about a boy who returns a lost wallet found in a danfo. We will read paragraph by paragraph and identify the main idea. For example, when the boy returns the wallet with all the money inside, the owner rewards him with a new school bag. This shows that honesty brings blessings.
Class activity:
Students will read the passage in groups and then write a summary of each paragraph in their own words.
Evaluation questions:
What happened when the boy returned the wallet?
Why did the owner give him a new school bag?
What lesson can we learn from this story?
How would you summarize the second paragraph?
Summary:
Understanding stories helps us improve our reading skills and learn important values like honesty.

topics.title: Grammar: sequence of tenses
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify correct sequence of tenses.
The students should be able to convert sentences into reported speech.
Introduction:
We have learned about different verb tenses like past, present and future. Today we will see how to use them correctly when reporting what someone said.
Content:
Sequence of tenses means using the right tense when reporting speech. For example, if someone says 'I am going to Lagos', we report it as 'He said he was going to Lagos'. The present tense becomes past tense. We will practice with sentences about everyday activities like 'I bought plantain at the market' becoming 'He said he had bought plantain at the market'.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to change direct speech sentences into reported speech, using the correct sequence of tenses.
Evaluation questions:
Change 'I will visit Abuja next week' to reported speech.
What happens to present tense verbs in reported speech?
Convert 'She is cooking jollof rice' to reported speech.
Why is sequence of tenses important?
Summary:
Using the correct sequence of tenses makes our writing clear and shows good understanding of grammar rules.

topics.title: Grammar: adverbials
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of adverbials.
The students should be able to use adverbials correctly in sentences.
Introduction:
We have learned about adverbs that describe actions. Today we will study adverbials which give more information about when, where and how actions happen.
Content:
Adverbials are words or phrases that tell us about time, place or manner. Time adverbials tell when something happens like 'yesterday' or 'during the harmattan season'. Place adverbials tell where like 'at the market' or 'under the mango tree'. Manner adverbials tell how like 'quickly' or 'with care'. For example, 'The woman sold her tomatoes quickly at the market during the harmattan season.'
Class activity:
Students will create sentences using different types of adverbials to describe activities in their local environment.
Evaluation questions:
Give an example of a time adverbial.
What does a manner adverbial tell us?
Write a sentence with a place adverbial.
How do adverbials make sentences more interesting?
Summary:
Adverbials add important details to our sentences and make our writing more descriptive and clear.

topics.title: Vocabulary: registered words
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between formal and informal words.
The students should be able to use appropriate register in different situations.
Introduction:
We use different words when talking to different people in different situations. Today we will learn about formal and informal words and when to use each.
Content:
Registered words are words used in specific situations. Formal words are used in serious situations like exams or official letters. Examples are 'purchase' instead of 'buy', 'commence' instead of 'start'. Informal words are used with friends like 'dash' instead of 'give', 'chap' instead of 'eat'. For example, in a letter to your principal you would write 'I wish to purchase a new book' not 'I want to buy a new book'.
Class activity:
Students will match formal words with their informal equivalents and then create sentences showing when to use each type.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between formal and informal words?
Give a formal word for 'see'.
When would you use formal language?
What is the formal word for 'child'?
Summary:
Using the right register helps us communicate appropriately in different situations and with different people.

topics.title: Composition: descriptive essay
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to write a descriptive essay.
The students should be able to use sensory details in their writing.
Introduction:
We have read descriptive passages before. Today we will learn how to write our own descriptive essay about a favorite place using details that appeal to our senses.
Content:
A descriptive essay paints a picture with words. To write about 'My favourite place', we use sensory details - what we see, hear, smell, taste and touch. For example, describing a market: 'I see bright colored fabrics stacked high, I hear the loud bargaining voices, I smell the fresh fish from the cold room, I taste the roasted corn being sold, I feel the rough texture of the ground.' These details make our writing vivid and interesting.
Class activity:
Students will brainstorm sensory details about their favorite place and then write a paragraph describing it using these details.
Evaluation questions:
What are the five senses we can describe in an essay?
Why are sensory details important in descriptive writing?
Give an example of a detail that appeals to smell.
How does describing a place help the reader imagine it?
Summary:
Using sensory details makes our descriptive essays more vivid and helps readers clearly imagine the places we describe.

topics.title: Argument essay
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to write an argument essay.
The students should be able to present counter arguments effectively.
Introduction:
We have written descriptive essays before. Today we will learn how to write an argument essay presenting reasons why boarding school is better than day school.
Content:
An argument essay presents reasons to support a position. For 'Boarding school is better', we give reasons like more study time, better discipline, and stronger friendships. We also consider counter arguments like missing family and then respond to them. For example, 'Some people say boarding school students miss their families, but they learn to be more independent and make friends from different parts of Nigeria.'
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to list arguments for and against boarding school, then write one paragraph with a counter argument.
Evaluation questions:
What is the purpose of an argument essay?
Name one advantage of boarding school.
How do you respond to a counter argument?
What makes an argument strong?
Summary:
Writing argument essays helps us develop critical thinking skills and learn to present our ideas clearly and logically.

topics.title: Oral: consonant clusters
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to pronounce words with consonant clusters correctly.
The students should be able to identify words with str, spr, spl sounds.
Introduction:
We have practiced pronunciation of different sounds in English. Today we will focus on consonant clusters, specifically words starting with str, spr and spl.
Content:
Consonant clusters are two or more consonant sounds together in words. We will practice words like 'street', 'spring', 'split'. These clusters can be difficult for some Nigerian speakers. For example, 'street' has the str cluster at the beginning. We will practice by saying each sound separately at first, then blending them together. Words like 'strong', 'spray', 'splash' are common in everyday Nigerian English.
Class activity:
Students will practice saying tongue twisters with consonant clusters like 'She sells seashells by the seashore' and identify words with str, spr, spl clusters.
Evaluation questions:
What is a consonant cluster?
Give an example of a word with the str cluster.
How can we practice pronouncing difficult clusters?
Why is proper pronunciation important?
Summary:
Mastering consonant clusters helps us improve our spoken English and communicate more clearly with others.

topics.title: Literature: figures of speech
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify simile, metaphor and personification.
The students should be able to explain the effect of each figure of speech.
Introduction:
We have read poems with figurative language before. Today we will learn about three common figures of speech: simile, metaphor and personification.
Content:
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as', for example 'Her smile is bright as the sun'. A metaphor directly states one thing is another, like 'The classroom was a zoo during break time'. Personification gives human qualities to non-human things, like 'The old house groaned with age'. These figures of speech make writing more vivid and interesting. In Nigerian literature, we often see metaphors comparing things to natural elements like 'His anger was as hot as the harmattan wind'.
Class activity:
Students will read Nigerian poems and identify examples of simile, metaphor and personification, explaining what each comparison means.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
Give an example of personification.
How do figures of speech make writing more interesting?
Find a simile in the poem we read today.
Summary:
Understanding figures of speech helps us appreciate the beauty of language and understand deeper meanings in literature.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer BECE-style questions correctly.
The students should be able to identify areas needing further study.
Introduction:
We have covered many topics this term. Today we will practice with past BECE questions to prepare for the exam and see what we need to revise more.
Content:
We will practice different types of BECE questions including comprehension, grammar, vocabulary, literature and composition. For comprehension, we will read passages about Nigerian life and answer questions. For grammar, we will practice tense sequence, adverbials and reported speech. We will mark our answers together and discuss common mistakes. For example, many students forget to change tenses in reported speech or confuse formal and informal words.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to answer a set of BECE practice questions, then present their answers and reasoning to the class.
Evaluation questions:
What is the most common mistake in reported speech?
How do you identify the main idea in a comprehension passage?
What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
Why is it important to practice past questions?
Summary:
Regular practice with exam questions helps us build confidence and identify areas we need to improve before the actual BECE.
